scenes.title: Ramsey's four funds
lines: Ramsey Solutions recommends spreading your investments across four kinds of mutual funds: growth, growth and income, aggressive growth, and international.
Say that after years of saving, you retire with a million dollars, a quarter of it in each, here in four American Funds that fit those labels.

scenes.title: How far back the funds go
lines: Three of these funds go back decades. Capital World Growth and Income only started in 1993, so before 1994 its quarter uses New Perspective's returns, a global fund from the same family.
That gives a retirement starting every year from 1981 on. The first sixteen have had a full thirty years.
Ramsey's book The Total Money Makeover, which lays out this four-fund mix, came out in September 2003.

scenes.title: Retire in January 2000
lines: Say you retired in January 2000 and took eighty thousand dollars a year, raised with inflation, a quarter from each fund.
The dot-com crash came first. Then in 2008 all four funds lost between thirty-five and thirty-nine percent.
The money ran out in 2013, thirteen years in. An S&P 500 index fund on its own would have run out four years sooner.

scenes.title: Every retirement since 1981
lines: Here's every retirement that started from 1981 on, each taking eighty thousand of today's dollars a year.
All sixteen that have had a full thirty years made it, and every one ended with more than the million it started with.
But eight of the twelve that started from 1997 to 2008 have already run out, most within twenty years.

scenes.title: Retiring around the book: 2002 to 2005
lines: Look closer at the four retirements around the book's release, from 2002 to 2005.
Retiring in 2003, the first year gained thirty-one percent, and by 2007 the million had grown to almost one and a half. Even after 2008, it still has more than a million left.
Retiring one year earlier, in 2002, the first year lost seventeen percent. The money never got back to a million, and it ran out in 2021.
The 2004 and 2005 retirees went into 2008 with much smaller cushions. One has nineteen thousand dollars left, and the other ran out in 2025.

scenes.title: Another way: 8% of what's left
lines: Now take eight percent of whatever is there each January instead. The money can't run out, but the paycheck rises and falls with the market.
For the 2000 retiree, the first check was eighty thousand. By 2003 it was forty-six thousand, and after 2008 it never again topped forty-five.
In its leanest year it paid thirty thousand dollars.

scenes.title: Checking Ramsey's numbers
lines: That quote rests on three numbers. Here's each one for every retirement in the four funds since 1981.

First, a twelve percent return. Across all forty-five years, the four funds did average a little over twelve. But the typical thirty-year retirement got about eleven, and only three of the sixteen reached twelve.
Second, inflation of four percent. That one held up: inflation ran lower, about three percent since 1981, and no finished retirement saw four.

Third, a nest egg growing four percent a year. Taking eight percent of what's left, the typical one grew about two percent, and none grew four. With inflation that low, it barely kept pace, and retirees from 1997 to 2008 fell behind.

scenes.title: Every retiree's leanest year
lines: Here's the leanest year for every retirement so far, taking eight percent of what's left.
Among the sixteen finished retirements, the typical leanest year paid about fifty-eight thousand dollars. The worst, retiring in 1996, got by one year on forty-nine thousand.
Those who retired around 2000 have already had years between thirty and thirty-seven thousand.

scenes.title: Against an S&P 500 index fund
lines: How do the four funds compare with an S&P 500 index fund on its own, taking the same eighty thousand a year?
The S&P fund lasted in fifteen of the sixteen finished retirements. And ten of the twelve that started from 1997 to 2008 have run out, against eight for the four funds.
Taking eight percent of what's left, the four funds' typical leanest year was fifty-eight thousand dollars, against forty-four for the S&P fund.
At four percent instead of eight, neither ever ran out. And taking four percent of what's left, the typical retiree never got a check below the first one, forty thousand.

scenes.title: What the four funds show
lines: Spread across four funds, eight percent lasted for every retirement that has had thirty years, and ran out for many that started near the 2000 peak.
Taking eight percent of what's left kept the money going, but many years paid far less than the eighty thousand planned.
Four funds or one index fund: at eight percent, the order of the years decides.
